These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. - **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.

Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).

     --repo <owner/name> --item-file <path to that JSON>
   ```

   **You supply the judgment — which outcome, and the prose.** Everything below
   is how to choose; nothing below is yours to perform. If the command refuses,
   read what it says: it means this item is not yours to converge, and doing it
   by hand anyway is how an item ends up closed wearing a live status.

   Then **make the calls it printed, in the order given, changing nothing** — the
   bodies verbatim, the label sets exactly as written. They are computed, not
   suggested: each label set already carries every label the issue should still
   have, so writing your own is how one gets dropped. One step asks you to output
   a line in your reply; do that too, it is the run's only census record.

   | label | when |
   |---|---|
   | `task:status:done` | succeeded, nothing pending — close the issue |
   | a park | anything else — leave the issue open, wearing exactly one of the four below |

   A park is ONE label, and its kind says what you are asking
   a person for. Pick by the REMEDY, not by how the run felt:

   | sub-label | when |
   |---|---|
   | `task:status:needs-human-approval` | you succeeded and deliberately left an unmerged PR. Name it; the human merges or closes it |
   | `task:status:needs-human-action` | something outside the code must change before this can run: a secret, a scope, a routine's wiring, an input this item never carried |
   | `task:status:needs-human-decision` | you stopped mid-flight and what happens next is a choice — you ran out of time, or you exceeded the declared ceiling and someone must say whether that stands |
   | `task:status:needs-human-failure` | the run broke: a bug, a contract-forbidden shape, a malformed or forged item. Use this when you are unsure |

   **A convergence you could not perform at all is the failure park, and never
   anything else.** Not `decision` (that is for a choice you stopped in front
   of), not `action` (that is for something outside the code that must change
   first). This is not a judgment call: the failure park is the only one that
   HOLDS THE TASK'S LANE, and a run that could not converge must stop its task
   recurring until a person has looked. Choosing a lane-releasing park here is
   how one broken convergence became fourteen stranded items in a member repo,
   one a night, each looking like a fresh incident.

   **Pass `--pr` on any park a pull request or an issue would end**, not only on an
   approval, where it is required. It stamps `Ends-when: #<n> closed` on the item, and
   that is what makes the park end by itself: the janitor closes the item `done` when
   the target merges and `rejected` when it is closed unmerged. Without it the park
   stands until a person happens to read it. **Pass it on a `done` too when your run
   landed a pull request**: on an item carrying `Supersedes:`, the pull request you
   name is what the earlier ones were waiting to be replaced by, and the command
   plans their closes only when it is given one.

   **A marked issue needs no write-back at all**: it is the item, so the approval
   park it wears *is* the in-review state and the failure park *is* the report (which
   is why `--pr` is still required on an approval — a park nobody can act on is not
   a park). The standing status is also what stops the next scheduler run adopting
   the same issue again; clearing it is a person's decision, made after reading what
   the run said. Only an item filed under the older shadow model writes back to a
   different issue, and the command does that too.

   Only `task:status:needs-human-failure` (and a park whose kind cannot be decoded) holds the
   task's lane — while one is open the generator files no further occurrence of
   this task. The other three wait for their human while the schedule carries on,
   so leaving one open costs nobody but the person it names.

   The `claudinite-task-exec` record goes onto the item, in the same comment, and
   the command writes it — Actions logs expire and the item does not, so the item
   is where a record has to live. Nothing here is yours to print by hand.

7. **Capture this session before you end it.** Last step, after the item is
   converged, and run it whichever way step 6 went:

   ```bash
   CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE=<n> node <engine>/hooks/session-end-command.mjs
   ```

   That runner invokes whatever session-end steps this repo's declared packs
   contribute; it knows nothing about what any of them do, and a repo that
   contributes none does nothing. Nobody is sitting in front of this session, so it
   ends by having its container reclaimed — precisely the ending that fires no
   `SessionEnd` hook. Left to the hook, every unattended run would leave no record
   of itself anywhere: not of the skills it loaded, not of the checks that caught
   something, not of how the work actually went, and not of the record you just
   printed. `CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE` is what files those logs under the item that
   ran, rather than under nothing.

   It cannot fail your run — the item is already converged and this changes nothing
   on GitHub. If it reports an error, **say so plainly in your final message** and
   end anyway.

## The one standing bound

You execute **this one item and nothing else**. Never list other work items,
never sweep the queue, never act on a second issue in this session — however
obviously stuck another one looks. Recovery is code that runs elsewhere, and a
session that helps out is how one item becomes three duplicate PRs.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

trigger — so a comment that only restates the last one wakes this task again tomorrow, and again

Before writing anything, read the issue's comments and find the most recent one this task posted

you are about to take is the one that comment already announced, **post nothing and change nothing**

<its date>' }`. Closing is never a repeat: it changes the issue's state and ends the sequence.

The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.

{"number":379,"title":"Dev console for scripted sim accounts, then the Appetize preview","body":"Tracking issue for two initiatives run as one chain: a **dev console** that drives four
simulated accounts against the real backend, and — gated on a human validation of that
console — the **Appetize preview** of the Android app (#99).

The end state of the console, and why it is shaped this way, is `docs/DEV-CONSOLE.md`
(#380). This issue holds the plan; it is append-only from here.

## Why the console comes first

Nothing in this repository has ever observed the backend working. `app/`'s 21 tests and
`dev/requirements/`'s 70 cases all run against scripted fakes; the functions' 14 tests are
pure-logic. Hyperlocal delivery cannot be observed with one client — the product *is* who
else was near you — so the first real proof of the backend needs several clients at once.
That instrument is worth more than a demo link, and the demo link is better once it exists.

## Decisions taken (2026-09-06)

| decision | choice |
|---|---|
| demo/console backend | reuse `shouts-whispers-dev` |
| preview sign-in | email/password demo account (the app has only Google Sign-In today) |
| seeding | scripted sim actors from the console, not a static seeder |
| console stack | Flutter web, `dev/console/` |
| console spec | its own suite, `dev/console/requirements/` |
| console access | Firebase Hosting on the dev project |
| time control | real-time against dev; compressed against the emulator |
| Android app id | keep `com.shoutsandwhispers.shouts_and_whispers` |

## The plan

Phase 0 — out-of-band setup, human, front-loaded.

- [ ] #382 — Firebase console steps, five accounts, Hosting, and the two repository secrets

Phase 1 — the stack, merged as a chain, each link blocked behind the last.

- [ ] #380 — the design doc
- [ ] #383 — sim-time wire contract and its four guards: server, rules, checks
- [ ] #384 — console package, plan model, plan editor, and its requirements suite
- [ ] #385 — replay engine and observation views, real-time against dev
- [ ] #386 — compressed mode against the emulator suite
- [ ] #387 — the dev deploy workflow and Hosting config

Phase 2 — execution.

- [ ] #388 — dispatch the deploy, confirm the console serves, post its URL
- [ ] #389 — human validation gate. Nothing below starts until this closes.

Phase 3 — the Appetize preview (#99), released by that gate.

- [ ] #390 — email/password sign-in path in the app, with its requirement leaves
- [ ] #391 — google-services Gradle plugin and the Appetize build workflow
- [ ] #392 — dispatch the build, upload, capture the URL, document it
- [ ] #393 — human confirmation that the preview is usable end to end
- [ ] #394 — retrospective, held until 2026-10-05

## Expected human gates

Three: the phase-0 checklist (#382), the console validation gate (#389), and the preview
confirmation (#393). Every other link carries an automerge policy predicting its own folder,
so a park anywhere else means a change reached further than this plan predicted — which is
the speed bump working, not an error to route around.

## Two deviations from the corpus, recorded deliberately

**Workflows rather than Claudinite tasks** for the two deploy paths (#387, #391), against
claudinite-growth's rule preferring a task. The vendored executor passes exactly one secret
to a run (`CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN`), so no queue run can reach `FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT` or
`APPETIZE_API_TOKEN`. A dispatchable workflow is the only mechanism in this repository that
can; the chain's execution links dispatch it and read its conclusion, which they *can* do.

**The console's `sim` capability is a legacy-tolerance-shaped risk that is not scaffolding.**
It is permanent — the emulator mode needs it for as long as the console exists — so it ships
with four independent guards instead of a removal date. #394's retrospective reads the strip
log to check that none of them has been load-bearing.

## What was measured before planning (2026-09-06)

- `cd app && flutter test` — 21 passed
- `cd dev/requirements && python3 run_requirements.py` — 70 passed
- `cd firebase/functions && npm run build && npm test` — clean, 14 passed
- `node --test .claudinite/local/packs/shouts-and-whispers/pack.test.mjs` — 24 passed
- Whether `shouts-whispers-dev` exists and is deployed: **unverified**. Firestore's REST
  API answers `403 CONSUMER_INVALID` identically for a project that does not exist, and
  `cloudfunctions.net` is egress-blocked from the session that planned this. #382's first
  checkbox settles it.

{"number":382,"title":"Console and secret setup for the dev console and the Appetize preview","body":"Everything under #379 that only a person can do, front-loaded so no later step waits on it.
Work top to bottom; the background is below the list.

- [ ] Confirm the project `shouts-whispers-dev` exists — [Firebase console](https://console.firebase.google.com/project/shouts-whispers-dev/overview)
- [ ] Upgrade it to the Blaze plan — [Usage and billing](https://console.firebase.google.com/project/shouts-whispers-dev/usage)
- [ ] Set a monthly budget alert on the project so an accident is capped — [Budget](https://console.firebase.google.com/project/shouts-whispers-dev/usage/details)
- [ ] Enable the Email/Password provider — [Sign-in method](https://console.firebase.google.com/project/shouts-whispers-dev/authentication/providers)
- [ ] Add the user `sim1@shoutsandwhispers.test` with a password you keep — [Users](https://console.firebase.google.com/project/shouts-whispers-dev/authentication/users)
- [ ] Add `sim2@shoutsandwhispers.test` with the same password — [Users](https://console.firebase.google.com/project/shouts-whispers-dev/authentication/users)
- [ ] Add `sim3@shoutsandwhispers.test` with the same password — [Users](https://console.firebase.google.com/project/shouts-whispers-dev/authentication/users)
- [ ] Add `sim4@shoutsandwhispers.test` with the same password — [Users](https://console.firebase.google.com/project/shouts-whispers-dev/authentication/users)
- [ ] Add `demo@shoutsandwhispers.test` with a different password — [Users](https://console.firebase.google.com/project/shouts-whispers-dev/authentication/users)
- [ ] Post the two passwords to this issue, or say here where they are kept
- [ ] Enable Hosting on the project — [Hosting](https://console.firebase.google.com/project/shouts-whispers-dev/hosting/sites)
- [ ] Press Generate new private key and keep the JSON file it downloads once — [Service accounts](https://console.firebase.google.com/project/shouts-whispers-dev/settings/serviceaccounts/adminsdk)
- [ ] Paste that whole JSON as the secret `FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT` — [Repository secrets](https://github.com/missingbulb/ShoutsAndWhispers/settings/secrets/actions)
- [ ] Create an Appetize account — [appetize.io](https://appetize.io/)
- [ ] Copy the API token from the account page, where it is shown under API
- [ ] Paste it as the secret `APPETIZE_API_TOKEN` — [Repository secrets](https://github.com/missingbulb/ShoutsAndWhispers/settings/secrets/actions)

## Done when

Opening [Users](https://console.firebase.google.com/project/shouts-whispers-dev/authentication/users)
lists five accounts, and
[Repository secrets](https://github.com/missingbulb/ShoutsAndWhispers/settings/secrets/actions)
lists both `FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT` and `APPETIZE_API_TOKEN`.

## Why each of these

**The project and Blaze.** Whether `shouts-whispers-dev` exists at all is unverified — the
session that planned #379 could not tell an absent project from a permission denial, and
`cloudfunctions.net` was egress-blocked. Blaze is not a preference: Cloud Functions cannot
be deployed on Spark, and this product's entire delivery path is a Cloud Function
(`docs/DESIGN.md` §4). Blaze keeps Spark's free allowances, so an idle dev project costs
about nothing — but it attaches a billing account, which is what the budget alert is for.

**Email/password and the five accounts.** The app has only Google Sign-In today, which
uses Android Credential Manager and therefore Google Play services — which an Appetize
emulator device may not have. Email/password is the path that does not depend on it. Four
`sim*` accounts are what the console drives; `demo@` is what a visitor to the Appetize
preview signs in as. The four sims share a password because the console asks for one
password and signs in all four; `demo@` differs because its password ends up in the public
README.

**Where the passwords go.** The console is deployed publicly on the dev site, so its
bundle must not carry them — the operator types them once and the browser keeps them
(`docs/DEV-CONSOLE.md`). Nothing automated needs the sim passwords; they are for whoever
drives the console.

**Hosting.** How the console is reached. Without it, validating the console means having a
Flutter toolchain and a checkout, which was the option this plan chose against.

**`FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT`.** What deploys functions, rules and the Hosting site from an
unattended run — and, via #395, what generates the app's Firebase client config without
anyone running `flutterfire configure` on a machine. Without it every deploy is a person at
a terminal.

**`APPETIZE_API_TOKEN`.** What uploads the APK. Only the last link of #379 needs it, but
it is here because a secret created late is a chain that stops for a person late.

## Changed 2026-09-06

A `flutterfire configure` step was here, asking for a local terminal there isn't one of.
It is now #395, a dispatchable workflow that reads `FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT` and commits
the generated config — which is also what `docs/ENVIRONMENTS.md` asks for, since dev client
config is committed and only prod's is injection-only.

{"number":99,"title":"Get the app running on Appetize.io (browser-based device preview)","body":"## Goal

Make the Flutter client in `app/` runnable in the browser via [Appetize.io](https://appetize.io/), so anyone can launch and interact with it on a simulated device without a local Flutter toolchain, a Firebase CLI, or a device. A shareable live demo link alongside the existing golden gallery in `dev/requirements/`.

Moved here from missingbulb/HelloWorldFlutterApp#1, which raised the same idea against a repo that has no native platform projects at all. This repo is the better home: `app/android/` and `app/ios/` already exist, so the original blocker there doesn't apply here.

## What stands in the way here instead

Appetize runs **native builds** — an Android `.apk`/`.aab` or an iOS simulator `.app`/`.zip`. Producing one for this app is not just `flutter build apk`, because the client is Firebase-backed:

1. **`lib/firebase_options.dart` is a committed placeholder that throws** until someone runs `flutterfire configure` (README, "Firebase setup"). An APK built as-is would crash on launch. The build needs real dev-project config (`google-services.json` + generated options).
2. **Google sign-in needs the signing key's SHA-1 registered** in the Firebase console. Whatever keystore CI signs the Appetize build with — debug or a dedicated demo key — its fingerprint must be added, or auth fails inside the preview.
3. **The app is location-first.** It wants a GPS fix before you can send, and reports presence heartbeats while foregrounded. Appetize sessions can inject a mocked location, but a demo where a single visitor is alone in a geohash cell shows an empty feed — the preview needs either seeded nearby presence/messages in the dev project, or a scripted location so visitors land where there's traffic.

## Proposed work

1. **Decide the backend the demo talks to** — the existing dev project, or a separate throwaway `shouts-whispers-demo`. Anything a browser visitor sends lands in real Firestore, so this should not be a project anyone depends on.
2. **Build the artifact** — `cd app && flutter build apk --debug` (Android first; no Apple signing needed). Do it in CI, not a sandbox, so the Firebase config can come from secrets rather than being committed.
3. **Upload to Appetize** — create an account, get an API token:
   ```bash
   curl https://api.appetize.io/v1/apps \
     -F "file=@app/build/app/outputs/flutter-apk/app-debug.apk" \
     -F "platform=android" \

## What stands in the way here instead

Appetize runs **native builds** — an Android `.apk`/`.aab` or an iOS simulator `.app`/`.zip`. Producing one for this app is not just `flutter build apk`, because the client is Firebase-backed:

1. **`lib/firebase_options.dart` is a committed placeholder that throws** until someone runs `flutterfire configure` (README, "Firebase setup"). An APK built as-is would crash on launch. The build needs real dev-project config (`google-services.json` + generated options).

[{"id":5561710722,"body":"## Appended 2026-09-06 — a step handed to a human that a mechanism can do

The plan above assumed the owner could run `flutterfire configure` on a local machine. There isn't one — this repository is worked from Claude Code on the web. That step was the most expensive kind of block basics names: work handed to a person that an agent could have taken.

It also contradicted `docs/ENVIRONMENTS.md`. Dev client config is **committed** by that contract; only prod's is injected by a release pipeline. #382 asked for the files as attachments and #391 said they are "never committed" — both wrong for dev.

What changed:

- **New link #395**, released by #382 alone: a dispatchable workflow that authenticates with `FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT`, registers the Android and web apps if the project has none, and opens a PR committing `app/lib/firebase_options.dart` and `app/android/app/google-services.json`.
- **#385 now waits on #395** as well as #384 — the console signs four accounts into the real project and needs the web app registration.
- **#391** no longer materializes config from secrets; it builds against the committed dev config.
- **#382** loses the `flutterfire` step and gains a budget-alert step, since Blaze attaches a billing account.

Blaze itself stands and is not a preference: Cloud Functions cannot be deployed on Spark, and `sendMessage` is this product's entire delivery path. I could not re-verify that against Google's documentation — `firebase.google.com` is egress-blocked from these sessions, as `docs.appetize.io` is — so it rests on the repository's own README rather than a fresh reading.

Which route #395's workflow can actually take is likewise unverified for the same reason: it tries the Firebase CLI non-interactively first, falls back to the Management REST API, and reports which worked.

{"number":390,"title":"Email/password sign-in path in the app","body":"Blocked-by: #389
Model: opus
Automerge: under:app; under:dev/requirements

First link of the Appetize half of #379, released by the validation gate. Read #389's
closing comment first: if it closed with the console judged broken, that is not a release —
converge as `action` and say so.

## Why the app needs this at all

`FirebaseAuthAdapter` offers only Google Sign-In, which in `google_sign_in` v7 goes through
Android Credential Manager and therefore Google Play services. An Appetize emulator device
may not carry Play services, and the sign-in would fail in a way the plugin reports as a
user cancellation (its own README says configuration errors surface as `canceled`). Nothing
about the preview works if the visitor cannot sign in, so the preview needs a path that does
not depend on Play services at all.

## What to build

An email/password sign-in on `AuthPort` beside `signInWithGoogle`, implemented in
`FirebaseAuthAdapter` with `signInWithEmailAndPassword`, and a sign-in screen that offers
both. Errors map to the port's existing `SignInException` shape rather than leaking
`FirebaseAuthException` into the UI — the ports boundary is the flutter pack's rule and an
import-scan test enforces it.

This is a product change, not a demo flag: it ships in the app for everyone. Decide
deliberately whether the second path is always visible or only when the account exists, and
say which you chose and why in this issue.

## Its spec

New leaves in `dev/requirements/requirements.md` — doc-first, red before green: the sign-in
screen's resting state with both options, and the driven behavior of an email sign-in
reaching the port. Propose the new goldens; the sign-in screen's existing golden will move,
and a moved golden is an owner decision — surface actual, expected and diff in this issue
and ask before re-baselining it.

## Done when

`cd app && flutter analyze && flutter test` and `cd dev/requirements && flutter test` are
green, and the moved golden has been approved in this issue rather than quietly regenerated.
